home.title: GPU Unlock — supported NVIDIA cards, measured speedups, install steps
home.description: Which NVIDIA cards the GPU Unlock kernel modules support across Ampere, Ada and Turing (RTX 20 series), what same-card benchmarks actually measured, and how to install each one.
home.h1: Unlock NVIDIA SM speed-select, with the numbers attached
home.lead: Three upstream kernel modules let consumer GeForce cards reach tensor throughput NVIDIA reserves for other parts. This site collects what they support, what was measured on the same card before and after, and what breaks.
home.statIdsNote: Across AD102, AD103, GA102, GA103, GA104, GA106, TU102, TU104 and TU106. Acceptance is not the same as a confirmed result.
home.statMeasuredNote: RTX 4090, RTX 4070 Ti SUPER and RTX 2080 Ti. Everything else rests on user reports or is untested.
home.statGainNote: f16/f32 and bf16/f32 on RTX 4090. FP32 and INT8 were never rate-limited and do not move.
home.whatBody: The module enables the SM speed-select override before the stock NVIDIA driver binds. It runs from the initramfs, so the driver never sees the card in its locked state. That ordering is the whole mechanism — loading the module after the driver has bound cannot work.
home.whatWarnTitle: Hardware risk is real and documented
home.whatWarnBody: The unlock writes speed-select registers and performs an FLR before the driver loads. Keep an unmodified stock boot entry, validate one cold boot before making anything persistent, and treat the AD103 path as experimental — it was validated on a single card.
home.benchBody: Every row below compares stock and unlocked on the same card with the same binary. Modes that were already at full rate are omitted here and shown in full on the benchmarks page.
home.seeAllBench: All benchmark rows, including the paths that did not change
home.cardsBody: Grouped by what is actually known, not by what the module accepts.
home.cardCount: All {count} cards, including untested and unsupported IDs
home.startStep1: Check that your card is in the accepted list, and how well it is known
home.startStep2: Read the install order — the initramfs step is not optional
home.startStep3: Read the failure modes before you flash anything
home.upstreamBody: This site documents these repositories; it does not fork them.
home.upstreamAmpere: the Ampere module: GA102, GA103, GA104, GA106 (v1.0.0)
home.upstreamAda: the Ada fork: adds AD102 RTX 4090 and an experimental AD103 canary (v1.1.1)
home.upstreamTuring: the Turing module: TU102, TU104, TU106 (RTX 20 series); only the 2080 Ti is measured

statusExplain.measured: A fork published stock-vs-unlocked numbers from one card with the same binaries.
statusExplain.reported: Someone filed a compatibility report. The forks did not independently revalidate it.
statusExplain.partial: The override applies but tensor throughput stays where it was.
statusExplain.untested: The module accepts the device ID. Nobody has published a result.
statusExplain.unsupported: Deliberately not in the accepted list.

gpus.idsTitle: How to check your own card
gpus.idsBody: Run `lspci -nn | grep -i nvidia` and match the `10de:xxxx` device ID against the list above. GeForce and CMP GA102/GA104 IDs are in the Ampere/Ada list; professional RTX A-series and data-centre parts are not. AD102 accepts only the RTX 4090, and AD103 is limited to the exact RTX 4070 Ti SUPER canary address. On RTX 20 series cards the accepting module is `turing_unlock`, and AD102/GA102 IDs mean nothing to it.

device.benchNote: Same card, same binary, stock versus unlocked. Modes that did not change are reported too — an unlock that does not move a path is a fact worth having.
device.noBench: No same-card measurement has been published for this card. Its status comes from user compatibility reports, not from a benchmark run under the maintainers' control.

bench.title: Benchmarks: stock versus unlocked
bench.description: Every same-card stock-vs-unlocked measurement published upstream, including the tensor modes that did not change, the FP8 CUTLASS pair that measured 1.0029×, and the RTX 2080 Ti cuBLAS table from the Turing fork.
bench.methodBody: The RTX 4090 rows come from a register-resident MMA issue-rate loop run at 20,000 iterations and three repetitions per mode, best-of-three reported. The RTX 4070 Ti SUPER rows come from the fork's tensor-modes-comparison.json, 66 SMs, driver 580.178.04, 240 W cap, 20,000 iterations and three repetitions, with all-one inputs across eight independent chains. The FP8 pair is a separate CUTLASS 4.8.1 profiler run on one sm_89 kernel. The RTX 2080 Ti rows are the Turing fork's README table: cuBLAS FP16 GEMM with FP32 accumulate, 250 W, driver 575.51.03, four M.N.K sizes, measured on a Dell 22 GB card. The README states TFLOPS directly and gives percent of a 56.9 TF/s peak in parentheses, which the author takes from the NVIDIA Turing whitepaper; those TFLOPS are quoted here unchanged. The README gives no iteration count, so none is shown.
bench.fp8Title: The FP8 pair that did not move
bench.fp8Body: The fork measured a matched E4M3 FP8 input, FP32 accumulate 4096³ GEMM on the 4070 Ti SUPER with the same CUTLASS profiler binary, one kernel, 10 warmups and 20 profiling iterations, requiring device-reference verification. Both runs passed their reference checks.
bench.readTitle: How to read a ratio of 1.00×
bench.readBody: A 1.00× row is not a failed unlock. It says that particular path was never rate-limited, so the override had nothing to restore. If you benchmark your own card and see 1.00× on the mode you care about, the unlock may well have applied correctly and simply does not help that workload.

install.title: Install GPU Unlock
install.description: The install order that matters: build locally, let the package put the right module (gpu_unlock or turing_unlock) in the initramfs before nvidia, opt in on the kernel command line, and only then make the boot entry persistent.
install.riskBody: The module writes speed-select registers and performs an FLR before the NVIDIA driver binds. Keep a stock boot entry. Validate a cold boot before making anything persistent. The AD103 path is experimental and was validated on one card. The Turing flow does the same, and its README warns that tensor cores draw very high power and that unlocking them may damage your hardware.
install.verifyBody: The module logs its decisions to the kernel ring buffer. Check the log and confirm the driver bound the card afterwards.
install.disableBody: Remove gpu_unlock.targets= from the kernel command line for Ampere/Ada, or turing_unlock.targets= for the RTX 20 series; for a one-off boot, delete it in the bootloader's edit screen. Removing the packages also removes the module and the initramfs drop-ins.
install.repoAmpere: Ampere: GA102, GA103, GA104, GA106. No Ada support.
install.repoAda: Ada: adds AD102 RTX 4090 and the experimental AD103 canary, and keeps the Ampere device list.
install.repoTuring: Turing: the RTX 20 series (TU102, TU104, TU106) via a separate module, turing_unlock. Ampere/Ada modules do not touch these cards.
